clue.text: Sailor has to understand aim and…

parts.note: a tar is a sailor, short for tarpaulin
to get something is to understand it, as in 'I get it'

explanation.surface: A seaman must grasp his goal, and the sentence runs on into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: The trailing dots link this clue to 4 across in the surface only; 'and' is a link word here.
explanation.definitionFit: A goal you aim at is the mark you set out to hit, a synonym.

clue.text: Paganini would do this and acknowledge applause

explanation.surface: A violinist bowing after a performance.
explanation.walkthrough: Paganini was a violin virtuoso, so he would literally pick up his bow.
explanation.definitionFit: A violinist picks up a bow to play, and a performer bends at the waist to accept clapping.

clue.text: The German turned spray on plant

parts.note: der is a German word for 'the'
to pepper is to spray, as with shot

explanation.surface: A German man aims a spray at his greenery.
explanation.definitionFit: A capsicum is a plant grown for its fruit, an example of a plant.

parts.note: ER is Elizabeth Regina, the Queen, plus the possessive S

explanation.surface: Is this the Queen's English? No, it's Scots.
explanation.walkthrough: Usually the Gaelic of Ireland, the word is also used for Scottish Gaelic.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gaelic language spoken in the Highlands has been called by this name.

indicators.note: move tells us the letters of the next words are shifted into a new order

explanation.surface: Troops march onward towards the Alps, carrying on from the previous clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'move' rearranges all eight letters of ON TO ALPS.
explanation.definitionFit: Platoons are military units made up of soldiers, so the plural noun stands for the troops themselves.

parts.note: the word left with its letters thrown out of order gives felt

explanation.surface: A one-word question about fabric being missed.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as wordplay, an anagram of LEFT, and it builds the clue word 'felt'.
explanation.definitionFit: Something excluded or skipped has been omitted, a synonym.

clue.text: Short 19 in kinky stilettos — they might put 21 downs through their paces

definitions.text: they might put 21 downs through their paces

indicators.note: in puts the short cleric inside the rearranged shoes

parts.note: P is a short form of the answer to 19 across, a cleric

explanation.surface: A cleric in kinky heels, as if from a tabloid.
explanation.walkthrough: 21 down is MIRAGE, the French fighter jet. 'kinky' shuffles STILETTOS into TESTILOTS, and 'in' puts P inside.
explanation.definitionFit: These aviators fly new aircraft to put them through trials.

clue.text: A religious vet on an African beast

indicators.note: on means placed after the approval word in a down entry

parts.note: to vet is to check and approve, to OK
pi is short for pious, religious

explanation.surface: A devout animal doctor attending an African animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vet' looks like an animal doctor, but it means approve.
explanation.definitionFit: This striped relative of the giraffe lives in Central African forests.

indicators.note: changing signals the letters of the cleric are changed around

parts.note: 19 refers to the answer to 19 across, a cleric

explanation.surface: A clergyman turns into a demon.
explanation.definitionFit: An elf or impish spirit is a mischievous supernatural creature, like a goblin.

clue.text: Knocked back drink after strange row

indicators.note: after places the reversed drink behind the strange word

parts.note: rum means odd or strange

indicators.note: knocked back means the drink is turned back to front

parts.note: to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: Downing a drink after an odd quarrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocked back drink' sounds like downing a glass, but it turns SUP into PUS.
explanation.definitionFit: A noisy disturbance or commotion is a row, a synonym.

clue.text: It's a very easy thing to feed young goats at first

indicators.note: at first places the young goats at the front of the charade, before the feeding word

parts.note: kids are young goats
to stuff is to feed someone to the full

explanation.surface: Feeding baby goats is a doddle.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads 'feed' then 'young goats', but 'at first' puts KIDS ahead of STUFF.
explanation.definitionFit: A child's task is proverbially simple, so the phrase means a trivial job.

indicators.note: around means the performer's word goes round the other piece

parts.note: the star is the lead performer in a show
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A dance step circles a lead actor.
explanation.definitionFit: Each step in a staircase is a single tread, so the word names one step.

parts.note: a Yankee is a type of bet: eleven combined wagers on four horses

explanation.surface: Asking whether to assist an American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yankee' wants to be an American; in betting shops it is a multiple bet covering four selections.
explanation.definitionFit: To aid someone, especially in wrongdoing, is to assist them, a synonym.

parts.note: to be up to something is to be ready for or capable of it
a point is a sharp tip, as of a pencil

explanation.surface: Partly prepared to give a gratuity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tip' looks like a gratuity, but it is the sharp end of something.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying something holds only partly, to a limited extent, is the idiom's meaning.

parts.note: leading lights suggests film stars, but means the attendants who lead people to seats with torches

explanation.surface: The great stars of film.
explanation.definitionFit: Cinema attendants show patrons to their seats by torchlight.

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a work
to sit for a portrait is to pose

explanation.surface: Someone resists both labour and modelling.
explanation.definitionFit: To resist or contest something is to set oneself against it, a synonym.

clue.text: Bloomers found in many Dutch fields

definitions.text: Bloomers found in many Dutch fields

parts.words: Bloomers found in many Dutch fields
parts.note: bloomers looks like knickers but means flowers, and the Netherlands is famous for fields of one spring bulb flower

explanation.surface: Underwear turning up all over the Dutch countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: These bulb flowers are grown commercially in vast Dutch fields, so they are the flowers meant.

parts.note: infantry looks like foot soldiers, but is read as infants

explanation.surface: How foot soldiers get carried about.
explanation.definitionFit: A baby buggy or stroller carries small children around.

parts.note: re means on or concerning
quests are searches for goals

explanation.surface: Appeals made about targets.
explanation.definitionFit: Requests and appeals are both asks for something, synonyms.

clue.text: Form of voting that's extremely suspect for a minister

parts.note: PR is proportional representation, a voting system
i.e. is the abbreviation for 'that is'

indicators.note: extremely means take just the outermost letters, first and last, of the word suspect

explanation.surface: An electoral system that looks dodgy to a government minister.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minister' is the clergy sense, not a government one; 'extremely' takes the first and last letters of 'suspect'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cleric who ministers to a congregation is a minister of religion.

parts.note: to tiddle is a childish word for to wee

explanation.surface: A small fish in a river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wee' looks like small, but it is the verb to urinate.
explanation.definitionFit: A small fish such as a stickleback is called by this childish word.

indicators.note: after puts the shuffled siesta letters following the noon letter

parts.note: M stands for meridies, midday, as in a.m. and p.m.

indicators.note: broke tells us the word siesta is broken up and its letters rearranged

explanation.surface: A painter interrupted his afternoon nap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'broke' looks like a past tense of interrupting the nap, but it is the anagram signal; M for noon comes from the Latin meridies, as in a.m. and p.m.
explanation.definitionFit: Henri Matisse was a French painter, an example of an artist.

clue.text: Motorway madness — something that appears when it's very hot!

definitions.text: something that appears when it's very hot!

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main motorway, written like MI
rage is madness or fury

explanation.surface: Road rage on the motorway in a heatwave.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds; its 1 doubles as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: An optical illusion of water seen in the desert heat is a classic example.

explanation.surface: A clergyman performs with a group.
explanation.walkthrough: 'band' looks like a music group, but it is a strip of colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A line or strip of colour is a band, a synonym.

parts.note: in cricket, the weakest batters come in at the bottom of the order, so they bat last

explanation.surface: Finally they get their turn at the crease.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the batting order puts the weakest batters, usually bowlers, at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket's lower-order batters, usually the bowlers, come in last.

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A puzzling ancient people.
explanation.walkthrough: Boudica led this ancient British tribe against Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: These were the British people of Boudica's revolt, a tribe of Iron Age Britain.

clue.text: Heads of elite cleaners refuse unwholesome linen

explanation.surface: Top cleaners decline to handle dirty bedsheets.
explanation.walkthrough: 'linen' is a colour here: the greyish-beige of unbleached linen.
explanation.definitionFit: This colour is the pale beige of unbleached linen, so the fabric names the shade.

parts.note: FT is the Financial Times, whose crossword this is, speaking of itself
re means about

explanation.surface: Anxiety over our own absence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'us' is the newspaper, the Financial Times, so FT; 'without' here means outside.
explanation.definitionFit: To fret is to be anxious, to worry, a synonym.

clue.text: Trendy drug before exercise is foolish

indicators.note: before puts the drug letter ahead of the exercise letters

parts.note: in means fashionable
E is short for ecstasy, the drug
PT is physical training, exercise

explanation.surface: Taking fashionable pills before a workout is silly.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone clumsy and lacking skill or sense is incompetent, a synonym.

clue.text: Agent crossed South Africa with misery

indicators.note: crossed suggests the letters are criss-crossed into a new order

explanation.surface: A spy travelled across South Africa feeling wretched.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crossed' looks like travelling across, but it shuffles SA with MISERY.
explanation.definitionFit: An envoy sent on a mission acts as someone's representative, an agent.

explanation.surface: A clergyman's remarkable ferns.
